SaleHoo helps online sellers discover potential suppliers and research products. Decide first whether you want to buy inventory in bulk or have a supplier ship individual orders. Write down your target country, product type, and maximum order size so you can compare suppliers on the same terms.

Compare supplier terms

Ask for a written quote covering the exact product variation, available stock, order minimum, shipping method, and damaged-item policy. For dropshipping, ask whether tracking is available and what appears on the packing slip. For wholesale, ask about reorder lead times and whether volume discounts require a larger commitment.

Order samples before committing

Compare samples for quality, packaging, and delivery time. Record the actual landed cost and test the support process if something arrives damaged. Check SaleHoo's current plans for what each subscription includes. For choosing what to source first, see Ecomhunt.

Compare a directory with an operating tool

When reviewing SaleHoo alternatives, identify the task you actually need help with. A supplier directory can help you find companies to contact. A product research tool can help you choose what to look for. An order-management tool can help once you have picked a supplier. Compare those jobs separately. For the directory, count how many relevant suppliers reply with usable quotes. For any integration, verify which stores and suppliers it supports before you depend on it. Compare directory alternatives.

Decide how orders will reach your customers

Before looking up a supplier in SaleHoo, decide who will hold the inventory and who will ship each order. In a wholesale arrangement, you typically buy a batch and hold it yourself or send it to a fulfillment partner. That gives you more control over stock, packaging, and dispatch. It also ties up cash until those units sell. In a dropshipping arrangement, the supplier ships individual orders. You can begin with less inventory, but the customer's experience depends more directly on the supplier's stock records and handling time.

Imagine you run a small shop for home coffee drinkers and want to add a compact scale. A wholesale supplier offers a carton of fifty units at a lower unit price. A dropshipping supplier can ship one unit at a time. The first quote may work if you already have steady demand and storage space. The second may suit a limited test if the supplier can deliver promptly and replace damaged units. Write down your expected volume and delivery promise before deciding which model fits.

Treat each option as a different workflow. With wholesale, ask where inventory will be stored, who will pick and pack it, and how you will manage unsold stock. With dropshipping, ask how orders are passed to the supplier, how stock changes reach your store, and who handles customer questions about a parcel. You can compare costs once you understand what each option expects you to do.

Create a supplier shortlist for one product

A wholesale supplier directory is most useful when the search starts with a clear brief. Write down the product type, destination country, expected order size, and the features that matter. For the coffee scale, those could include platform size, supported units, and what powers it. Include the exact packaging or accessory requirements if they affect what the customer will receive.

Look for suppliers that can serve the market and model you chose. A distributor might sell to stores in your country but require a business account and a minimum opening order. A dropshipping supplier might accept individual orders but ship only to selected regions. Put these requirements in your notes early. They can save time before you investigate every product in a supplier's catalog.

Record three to five candidates in a simple sheet. Use columns for the company name, product reference, location, order minimum, and contact method. Add a column for what you still need to confirm. A directory entry gives you a starting point. Ask the supplier directly about stock, shipping, and terms for the exact variation.

Send a request suppliers can answer accurately

Use the same written brief for every candidate. Say which product you want, where it needs to go, and how many units you expect to order. Ask for the quote in a named currency and for the product and shipping prices to appear separately. If the quote covers a particular date or destination, save that information beside the price.

Ask for the exact model and what comes in the box. A catalog photo might show accessories included only in a different package. A quote that says “digital scale” may refer to a smaller model than the sample you saw. Ask for the supplier's reference number and a recent photograph of the package. Then compare those details with what you plan to list.

For wholesale, request prices at realistic quantities and ask when a repeat order could ship. If the minimum order is fifty units, ask whether you can buy a paid sample or a smaller trial carton. For dropshipping, ask about stock visibility, order cutoffs, tracking, and the name or return address that appears on parcels. Find out how the supplier handles a shipment when the item sells out after a customer has paid.

Compare replies for clarity as well as price. A usable answer gives you enough detail to quote a delivery window and explain returns. If an answer leaves an important point open, ask one precise follow-up. Keep the response with the date so you can distinguish current terms from an older discussion.

Compare the cost of getting one order delivered

Start with the cost you pay for the product. Add the shipping you cover, packaging or fulfillment fees, payment or marketplace fees, and an allowance for returns or replacements. If duties or other charges may apply, check who pays them. The goal is to compare the amount left from a sale under each sourcing arrangement.

Suppose a scale sells for $36. In an example wholesale arrangement, the item and its share of inbound shipping cost $14. Packing and customer delivery cost $6, while selling fees and a returns allowance total $4. That leaves $12 before advertising and fixed costs. In an example dropshipping arrangement, the supplier charges $23 to deliver one unit and the same fees and allowance total $4. That leaves $9 before advertising and fixed costs. These figures illustrate the calculation. Use your own quotes and store records to make a buying decision.

Now include the costs that change when an assumption fails. What happens if five units in the carton are damaged or if orders arrive slowly and customers request refunds? If you pay for storage, include the period you expect to hold inventory. If a dropshipping supplier charges extra for remote areas, check how often your customers live in those areas. A delivered cost is useful when it reflects how you expect orders to work.

Keep wholesale cash flow visible. Paying for fifty items today and selling them over several months is different from paying one supplier invoice for each confirmed order. Set a budget for stock and leave room for a reorder if the product works. If you are unsure how quickly it will sell, compare a smaller trial with the savings on the larger carton.

Check a sample before writing the listing

Order the exact version you plan to sell. Record how long the parcel takes to arrive and what tracking the supplier provides. Photograph the package before opening it. Compare the contents with the written quote and check whether the instructions match the item. If the product arrives with a different accessory or label, ask whether the sample and future orders come from the same stock.

Use the sample as your customer would. For a coffee scale, check whether the platform fits common cups or brewers, whether the display remains visible with a cup on top, and whether the controls are easy to understand. Make only the claims you can support. An image showing a real mug on the scale can answer a fitting question more clearly than a general product photo.

Write down anything that will change the customer experience. A supplier may offer sturdy packaging but use a delivery method without tracking. The product itself may be good while the instructions are hard to follow. Some problems can be addressed with your own insert or guide. Others may justify trying a different supplier. Use the sample to identify which is which before paying for a larger order.

Plan for returns and stock changes

Ask what happens when the customer receives the wrong model or an item arrives damaged. Find out what evidence the supplier needs, who sends a replacement, and who covers the return shipping. If the supplier's policy gives you a short window to report problems, make sure your customer support process can collect the information in time.

For a dropshipping store, document what you will do when stock changes. Decide who checks availability and how quickly the listing should be paused if an item sells out. Set a process for customer updates if an order cannot ship on time. For wholesale, decide when to reorder and how much extra inventory you can afford. Review these decisions after the first few weeks of real orders.

Save the supplier's contact details, quote, delivery terms, and sample notes in one place. If a team member takes over an order, they should be able to see what was agreed without searching old messages. That record also helps you compare a new supplier later using the same questions.

Compare SaleHoo alternatives by the work you need done

If your main problem is finding companies to contact, compare supplier directories by how many relevant candidates you can turn into usable quotes. If your main problem is keeping inventory and orders in sync, compare integration tools by the stores, suppliers, and fulfillment steps they support. An attractive directory listing tells you little about how a store integration will work after launch.

Use the same sourcing brief across the services you compare. For the coffee scale, count candidates that can deliver the correct model to your target country. Track replies, total delivered cost, and willingness to provide a sample. Time the process so you can see whether the tool saves work once you include the checks you still have to do yourself. A general list of alternatives can help you find candidates for this comparison. SaleHoo Directory alternatives.

If you are still deciding which product to source, separate discovery from supplier selection. A tool like Ecomhunt can give you product ideas to investigate. A directory helps you find companies that may be able to deliver an item you already understand. To see how to build the shortlist before you contact suppliers, read the Ecomhunt product research guide.

Check SaleHoo Group Buy access before ordering

Confirm which product or subscription the offer covers, how long access lasts, and whether you can use the functions you need. Check how you will retain supplier notes or messages if access ends. If you expect an integration to manage orders, verify that it is part of the offer and works with your store setup. Compare the details with SaleHoo's current plans.

Try to define what a successful first week would look like. It might mean finding three suppliers, receiving two comparable quotes, and ordering one sample. That gives you a way to judge access based on a real task. If the plan includes tools your team will rarely use, weigh those against the cost and time required to do the work you actually need.

Frequently asked questions

Is SaleHoo useful for both wholesale and dropshipping? SaleHoo offers supplier discovery for both models. Look for suppliers whose terms match how you intend to buy and deliver orders. Confirm minimums and destinations directly.

Does a directory listing mean the supplier will serve my store? Use the listing to find a candidate. Ask about the exact item, shipping destination, stock, and any business requirements. A current written quote is more useful than a general directory description.

How do I compare quotes in different currencies? Convert them using a consistent rate and record the date. Check whether your payment provider adds a conversion fee. Compare the cost of delivering the same product to the same destination.

Should I ask about resale permissions? If the product carries a brand or you plan to sell it on a marketplace with product restrictions, check the supplier's authorization and the marketplace rules before listing it.

When should I move from a sample to a larger order? Review sample quality, delivery time, costs, and supplier communication first. A small initial order can give you more evidence about demand and support needs before you commit a larger budget.
